candidate.answerReason: The perpendicularity gives congruent right triangles ABP and BCQ, so CQ=BP=13. The length and right-angle conditions then give BC squared equal to 117; the other algebraic possibility violates BQ≤BC.

methods.label: Congruence and the Pythagorean theorem
methods.explanation:
The perpendicular segments connect two right triangles built on equal sides of the square. Comparing those triangles will give us the full length of \(CQ\).

The cases \(P=A\) or \(Q=B\) would make the perpendicular segments meet at \(B\), contradicting \(BR=6\). Thus \(ABP\) and \(BCQ\) are nondegenerate right triangles. Their acute angles \(\angle ABP\) and \(\angle BCQ\) are equal because their sides are respectively perpendicular. Also,
\[
\angle BAP=\angle CBQ=90^\circ,
\qquad AB=BC.
\]
Therefore \(\triangle ABP\cong\triangle BCQ\) by ASA. In particular,
\[
CQ=BP=BR+RP=6+7=13.
\]
Let \(RQ=x\), where \(0<x<13\). Then \(CR=13-x\). Applying the Pythagorean theorem to the two right triangles with right angle at \(R\) gives
\[
BC^2=36+(13-x)^2,
\qquad BQ^2=36+x^2.
\]
Triangle \(BCQ\) is right at \(B\), so
\[
169=BC^2+BQ^2
=72+(13-x)^2+x^2.
\]
Expanding and simplifying yields
\[
x^2-13x+36=0,
\qquad (x-4)(x-9)=0.
\]
We must choose the root compatible with the square. Since \(Q\) lies on \(AB\), we have \(BQ\le AB=BC\). The two squared-length expressions above therefore require \(x\le13-x\). This rules out \(x=9\), leaving \(x=4\) and \(CR=9\).

The square's area is its side length squared:
\[
BC^2=6^2+9^2=\boxed{117}
\]
square units, choice \(\mathrm{D}\).

methods.label: Measure one triangle's area two ways
methods.explanation:
The altitude \(BR=6\) lets us calculate the area of \(BCQ\) once its hypotenuse is known. Comparing this with the area calculated from its two legs will give a useful product of lengths.

Neither \(P=A\) nor \(Q=B\) is possible, because either case would force \(R=B\). The right triangles \(ABP\) and \(BCQ\) have equal sides \(AB=BC\), equal right angles at \(A\) and \(B\), and equal acute angles \(\angle ABP=\angle BCQ\), since the sides of those acute angles are respectively perpendicular. They are therefore congruent by ASA. Consequently,
\[
CQ=BP=6+7=13,
\qquad AP=BQ.
\]
Write \(s=AB=BC\) and \(t=AP=BQ\). These lengths satisfy \(0<t\le s\), since \(P\) lies on a side of the square.

Using \(CQ\) as the base of triangle \(BCQ\), its corresponding height is \(BR\), so its area is \(\tfrac12\cdot13\cdot6=39\). Its perpendicular legs also give area \(\tfrac12 st\). Thus
\[
st=78.
\]
The Pythagorean theorem in \(ABP\) gives
\[
s^2+t^2=13^2=169.
\]
Knowing both the sum of the squares and the product lets us find the sum and difference of the lengths:
\[
(s+t)^2=169+2(78)=325,
\]
\[
(s-t)^2=169-2(78)=13.
\]
Because \(s+t>0\) and \(s-t\ge0\),
\[
s+t=5\sqrt{13},
\qquad s-t=\sqrt{13}.
\]
Adding gives \(s=3\sqrt{13}\). Hence the square's area is
\[
s^2=(3\sqrt{13})^2=\boxed{117}
\]
square units, choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
